newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN OIL INDUSTRY AWAITS NEWS ON MARGIN HIKE.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN OIL INDUSTRY AWAITS NEWS ON MARGIN HIKE.

text.p: The oil industry on Friday said it still hoped to receive an across-the-board three cents a litre wholesale margin increase in November but economists said it might only get it on gasoline, if at all.
South African Petroleum Industry Association (Sapia) director Colin McClelland told Reuters he had not yet been briefed on the study a special Cabinet committee was appointed to undertake this week.
"But we trust that it will not delay the granting of the 1995 marketing of petroleum activities return (MPAR) that has been due since the beginning of this year," McClelland said.
"We have already indicated that we would be very willing to talk about new rules for the future, but existing arrangements should be applied in the meantime."

Sapia had been hoping the margin increase would be approved by Cabinet this week, but Cabinet Secretary Jakes Gervel said on Friday that it had been decided to appoint a ministerial committee to evaluate MPAR and the oil price formula.

Although Cabinet could still approve the margin increase for gasoline and diesel on October 23 in time for the November fuel price adjustment, recent steep rises in diesel prices because of world shortages could prompt Cabinet to only grant the margin for gasoline.
Econometrix economist Tony Twine told Reuters that this could be "a politically smart move" given the expected seven to eight cents increase in the diesel price next month.
By not increasing the margin on diesel, the differential between petrol and diesel prices would be re-established "by a few cents".
This would make diesel cheaper than petrol and would be welcomed by farmers, industry and bus and train operators.
McClelland said, however, said that the increase on both petrol and diesel was "part of the existing contractual position" between government and the oil industry and should be granted.
The need for the increases was highlighted by the fact that industry profits had moved back to the 1990 level of 800 million rand after peaking at 1.3 billion in 1993, he said.

Some industry officials were dismayed that yet another study was being commissioned on the oil industry but said it would re-open the debate on the extent to which the oil industry should be deregulated.
The most recent study into the industry by Izak Lamprechts of Stellenbosch University had found that deregulation was not an option for at least five years.
"But this is one of the few industries that is still regulated and it could hurt government in the eyes of consumers if it is seen to be continuing to fix prices," said one source.

The delay in granting the margin increase and continued delays in making a decision on the future of the industry could affect urgently needed investment decisions, especially on new refinery capacity, he said.
